newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's WTO entry "good for world", Brittan says.
newsitem.headline: China's WTO entry "good for world", Brittan says.

text.p: European Commission Vice President Sir Leon Brittan said on Monday that China's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO) still required tough negotiations but added it would be "good for the world".

"The Chinese will have to accept the obligations over a period of time and we're not talking about an indefinite period of time, so there's some tough bargaining to come," Brittan said on Hong Kong government radio.

Brittan said in Beijing on Friday that China had pledged support for European suggestions of a scenario in which China joins the WTO, accepting the most important obligations at the beginning and the others over a period of time.
"I have put that to the Americans and I hope very much that they will go along with that and that we renew negotiations with greater urgency and at a higher level," he said.
Beijing is seeking to join the WTO on the lenient terms of a developing country but faces resistance from Washington, which says the Chinese economy is too large.

Brittan, who is in Hong Kong for the three-day World Economic Forum which began on Monday, said the energy China was putting into its bid clearly showed its interest in joining the international trade body.
"Judging by the amount of effort they are making and the things that were said to me, that's clearly the case," he said.

"I think it would be good for the world but also good for China to have China in the WTO because if it comes in on the right terms and in a reasonable way, it will advance the process of opening up the Chinese economy and liberalising China itself."

China hoped to join the WTO at its foundation in January 1995 but failed after disagreements over terms of its entry, with the United States and several other developed nations insisting that economic reforms and greater market access were necessary conditions.

China, a founder member in 1948 of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) which was replaced by the WTO, withdrew after the communist takeover in 1949. It has tried to gain re-entry since 1986.

The re-election of U.S. President Bill Clinton has made a difference to the process, Brittan said, as the Chinese side was worried about a potential U.S. veto and had held off on any concrete action until after the poll.

Brittan said he had taken up the issue with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who is due in Beijing on Monday to lay the groundwork for a meeting between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders meeting in Manila later in the month.
